Estimating and interpreting Gaussian graphical models with the psychnets R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/gaussian-graphical-models.Rmd
gaussian-graphical-models.Rmd

Does the association between motivation and achievement persist once effort, prior achievement and other measured constructs are taken into account? This question arises when psychological and educational researchers examine interrelated characteristics such as self-efficacy, learning strategies, self-regulation and anxiety. Pairwise correlations may reflect associations shared with other scores, making them difficult to interpret. Network analysis examines such interdependence without assigning every construct a fixed role as predictor or outcome (Borsboom et al., 2021). A Gaussian graphical model (GGM) represents variables as nodes and conditional associations as edges, estimating partial correlations between pairs of variables while accounting for the remaining variables (Epskamp & Fried, 2018). An edge does not establish causality, and a missing edge does not prove that two constructs are unrelated.

GGMs are useful when researchers want to distinguish associations that remain after adjustment from those visible in an ordinary correlation matrix. For example, two learning strategies may be strongly correlated but have a much weaker partial correlation once motivation and self-regulation are included. Regularisation can set small estimated edges to zero and make a network easier to interpret, although the selected model need not be sparse. The resulting pattern depends on the variables, measurement scale, sample and estimation procedure. Researchers therefore need to consider the accuracy of estimated edges and the consequences of methodological choices, rather than interpreting a network diagram on its own (Epskamp et al., 2018; Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023; Williams & Rast, 2020).

Psychological networks have also been applied to educational questions about how learning processes operate together. Studies have examined associations among monitoring events during self-regulated learning, including how those events relate to phases of regulation (Malmberg, Saqr, Järvenoja, Haataja, et al., 2022; Malmberg, Saqr, Järvenoja, & Järvelä, 2022). Network approaches have likewise been used to study the relational and temporal aspects of self-regulation in academic writing (Saqr et al., 2021). These applications illustrate why the relationships among learning processes may be of interest alongside the levels of individual constructs (Saqr et al., 2024). The choice of network model must nevertheless match the research design: a cross-sectional GGM does not describe within-person change over time.

This article provides a worked example of a regularised GGM using five self-regulated learning construct scores from language-model-generated survey responses. It explains how to estimate and interpret partial-correlation edges, compare them with ordinary correlations, assess computational optimality, and describe node strength, expected influence and predictability. It then compares Pearson and Spearman estimation, applies a post-hoc edge threshold and fits a nonparanormal model. The aim is to support careful interpretation and reporting by applied researchers, not to draw conclusions about students from these generated responses.

library(psychnets)

The model

For variables X1,…,XpX_1, \ldots, X_p with covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, the inverse covariance matrix, or precision matrix, 𝐊=𝚺−1\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}, describes their conditional association structure. The partial correlation between XiX_i and XjX_j given the remaining variables is

ρij⋅rest=−KijKiiKjj, \rho_{ij \cdot \mathrm{rest}} = -\frac{K_{ij}}{\sqrt{K_{ii}K_{jj}}},

Under multivariate normality, Kij=0K_{ij} = 0 means that XiX_i and XjX_j are conditionally independent given the remaining variables. A non-zero partial correlation is represented by an edge. Its sign indicates the direction of the conditional association and its magnitude indicates its strength on the partial-correlation scale.

Sample partial correlations are subject to sampling variation, and small non-zero estimates may not reflect a reproducible association. The graphical lasso (Friedman et al., 2008) estimates the precision matrix while penalising the absolute values of its off-diagonal entries,

𝐊̂=argmin𝐊≻0{tr(𝐒𝐊)−logdet(𝐊)+λ∑i≠j|Kij|}, \widehat{\mathbf{K}} = \underset{\mathbf{K} \succ 0}{\operatorname{argmin}} \left\{ \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{K}) - \log\det(\mathbf{K}) + \lambda \sum_{i \ne j}|K_{ij}| \right\},

where 𝐒\mathbf{S} is the sample correlation matrix and λ\lambda controls the amount of shrinkage. Larger penalties can set more off-diagonal entries to zero, removing their corresponding edges. The penalty λ\lambda is selected from candidate values using the extended Bayesian information criterion (EBIC; Foygel & Drton, 2010),

EBIC⁡γ=−2ℓ(𝐊̂)+Elog⁡n+4Eγlog⁡p, \operatorname{EBIC}_{\gamma} = -2\ell(\widehat{\mathbf{K}}) + E\log n + 4E\gamma\log p,

Here ℓ\ell is the Gaussian log-likelihood, EE is the number of edges, nn is the sample size and pp is the number of nodes. The hyperparameter γ\gamma (0.5 by default) adds a complexity penalty beyond the usual BIC term. Larger values favour sparser networks, but the selected number of edges still depends on the data.

Data

SRL_GPT contains 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. Each variable is a construct score calculated as the mean of its items on a scale from 1 to 7. The responses were generated by a large language model (GPT) for a study of how these models complete psychological questionnaires (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). They provide an illustrative dataset for learning the method and must not be interpreted as observations of students.

  • Nodes: five construct scores, each treated as continuous:
    • CSU, cognitive strategy use;
    • IV, intrinsic value;
    • SE, self-efficacy;
    • SR, self-regulation;
    • TA, test anxiety.
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
head(SRL_GPT)
#>        CSU       IV       SE       SR   TA
#> 1 5.307692 5.666667 5.777778 5.333333 4.00
#> 2 5.846154 6.444444 6.000000 5.777778 4.00
#> 3 6.615385 6.666667 6.222222 6.333333 3.25
#> 4 5.692308 6.555556 6.333333 5.555556 4.50
#> 5 4.384615 5.555556 4.888889 4.777778 4.00
#> 6 4.846154 5.444444 5.666667 5.111111 3.50

Because the construct scores are averages of several items and have many distinct values, treating them as continuous is reasonable for this example. For analyses of item-level ordinal responses, polychoric correlations may be more appropriate (cor_method = "auto").

Which constructs are directly associated?

psychnet() with method = "glasso" estimates the EBIC graphical lasso. The defaults are Pearson correlations, pairwise-complete handling of missing values and γ=0.5\gamma = 0.5.

net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "glasso")
summary(net)
#> <psychnet> glasso network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 10   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.00861   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.21e-10
#>   edge weight: range [-0.350, 0.412], mean 0.174

The selected penalty is λ=0.00861\lambda = 0.00861. The fitted network retains all 10 possible edges among the five nodes, so regularisation has not removed any pairwise connection in this example. The partial correlations range from -0.350 to 0.412. The edge table gives the estimated weight of each pair:

as.data.frame(net)
#>    from to      weight
#> 1   CSU IV  0.41166866
#> 2   CSU SE  0.38290223
#> 3    IV SE  0.15992605
#> 4   CSU SR  0.35481359
#> 5    IV SR  0.31909443
#> 6    SE SR  0.20767208
#> 7   CSU TA  0.04906668
#> 8    IV TA  0.11058735
#> 9    SE TA  0.09871818
#> 10   SR TA -0.34985157

The four learning constructs are joined by positive edges. The largest positive partial correlation is between cognitive strategy use and intrinsic value (0.412), followed by cognitive strategy use and self-efficacy (0.383), and cognitive strategy use and self-regulation (0.355). These estimates indicate positive associations after adjustment for the other three constructs, rather than unadjusted pairwise relationships. Self-regulation and test anxiety have the only negative edge (-0.350), indicating that higher self-regulation is associated with lower test anxiety when the other variables are held constant. The remaining edges involving test anxiety are small and positive: CSU (0.049), SE (0.099) and IV (0.111). Their substantive importance should not be inferred from the presence of an edge alone.

How do partial correlations differ from correlations?

A marginal correlation describes the association between two variables without controlling for the others. The correlation network estimated with method = "cor" provides a useful comparison with the adjusted associations in the GGM.

as.data.frame(psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "cor"))
#>    from to      weight
#> 1   CSU IV  0.86099753
#> 2   CSU SE  0.83458495
#> 3    IV SE  0.78460033
#> 4   CSU SR  0.84743518
#> 5    IV SR  0.82163456
#> 6    SE SR  0.77913881
#> 7   CSU TA -0.13851086
#> 8    IV TA -0.11372136
#> 9    SE TA -0.09672104
#> 10   SR TA -0.30196344

The six correlations among the four learning constructs range from 0.779 to 0.861, considerably larger than their partial correlations, which range from 0.160 to 0.412. This reduction indicates that their pairwise relationships overlap with associations involving the other constructs. Test anxiety has a negative marginal correlation with each learning construct (-0.097 to -0.302), whereas its partial correlations with CSU, IV and SE are small and positive. Its partial correlation with self-regulation remains negative (-0.350). Thus, the adjusted results give a different account of how test anxiety relates to the constructs. They do not establish that self-regulation causes the other marginal associations.

Is the fitted network the optimum of its objective?

The graphical lasso uses numerical optimisation to estimate the network. Before interpreting the edges, it is useful to check whether the algorithm has converged sufficiently closely to the solution of its objective. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker optimality conditions provide such a check. certificate() reports the largest numerical violation of these conditions and returns certified = TRUE when that value is below 10−610^{-6}. This is a check on computational accuracy, not on the reliability of the estimated associations.

certificate(net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1 glasso 2.213389e-10  kkt      TRUE

The reported violation is 2.21×10−102.21 \times 10^{-10}, well below the stated tolerance. The estimated network therefore satisfies the numerical optimality check for the selected penalty. This result does not assess sampling uncertainty, model fit or the plausibility of the distributional assumptions.

Which constructs are most connected?

net_centralities() summarizes each node’s edges. Strength is the sum of absolute edge weights; expected influence is the signed sum, in which negative edges offset positive ones (Robinaugh et al., 2016).

net_centralities(net)
#>   node  strength expected_influence
#> 1  CSU 1.1984512         1.19845117
#> 2   IV 1.0012765         1.00127649
#> 3   SE 0.8492185         0.84921854
#> 4   SR 1.2314317         0.53172852
#> 5   TA 0.6082238        -0.09147935

Self-regulation has the highest strength (1.231), closely followed by cognitive strategy use (1.198). Cognitive strategy use has only positive edges, so its expected influence also equals 1.198. By contrast, the negative edge between self-regulation and test anxiety reduces the expected influence of self-regulation to 0.532. Test anxiety has the lowest strength (0.608) and a slightly negative expected influence (-0.091). Strength therefore identifies self-regulation as the most connected node in terms of absolute edge weights, while expected influence shows why the signs of those edges matter. These are descriptions of this fitted network, not evidence that changing a highly connected construct would change the others.

How well is each construct predicted by the others?

Predictability is the proportion of a node’s variance explained by its neighbours, R2R^2 (Haslbeck & Waldorp, 2018). For a GGM it follows from the precision matrix, Rj2=1−1/(KjjSjj)R_j^2 = 1 - 1/(K_{jj}S_{jj}), so net_predict() needs no further data.

net_predict(net)
#>   node     type metric predictability accuracy
#> 1  CSU gaussian     R2      0.8217840       NA
#> 2   IV gaussian     R2      0.7690346       NA
#> 3   SE gaussian     R2      0.7142811       NA
#> 4   SR gaussian     R2      0.7786477       NA
#> 5   TA gaussian     R2      0.1421163       NA

In this fitted model, the other nodes account for approximately 82% of the variance in cognitive strategy use (R2=0.822R^2 = 0.822), 78% in self-regulation, 77% in intrinsic value and 71% in self-efficacy. The corresponding value for test anxiety is much lower, at 14% (R2=0.142R^2 = 0.142). This suggests that the other four scores contain comparatively little information about variation in test anxiety in these generated responses, despite the negative self-regulation edge. Predictability is calculated in sample and should not be presented as out-of-sample predictive performance without validation.

What does the network look like?

cograph::splot() draws the fitted network. With psych_styling = TRUE, positive edges are green, negative edges red, edge width follows the absolute weight, and the ring around each node shows its predictability.

cograph::splot(net, psych_styling = TRUE)

The figure shows the dense positive cluster of the learning constructs and the single negative edge to test anxiety. Node positions come from a layout algorithm, and the distance between two nodes carries no statistical meaning.

Do the conclusions depend on the correlation estimator?

Spearman correlations use ranks and are less affected by skewed distributions and extreme values. Refitting with cor_method = "spearman" tests whether the structure depends on the Pearson estimator.

spearman_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "glasso",
                         cor_method = "spearman")
summary(spearman_net)
#> <psychnet> glasso network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 9   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.01882   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.67e-10
#>   edge weight: range [-0.237, 0.424], mean 0.192
as.data.frame(spearman_net)
#>   from to      weight
#> 1  CSU IV  0.41037571
#> 2  CSU SE  0.42434529
#> 3   IV SE  0.12821527
#> 4  CSU SR  0.32164519
#> 5   IV SR  0.34602908
#> 6   SE SR  0.18400655
#> 7   IV TA  0.07280225
#> 8   SE TA  0.07509761
#> 9   SR TA -0.23654039

The Spearman-based model selects a larger penalty (λ=0.01882\lambda = 0.01882) and retains 9 edges. All six positive edges among the learning constructs remain, as does the negative edge between self-regulation and test anxiety, although its weight changes from -0.350 to -0.237. The smallest Pearson-based edge, CSU–TA (0.049), is absent. These results suggest that the main pattern is similar under the two correlation estimators, while the weaker connections involving test anxiety are more sensitive to the choice of estimator.

What does a post-hoc threshold change?

A post-hoc threshold removes estimated edges whose absolute weights fall below a specified value. This may simplify a display but changes the reported graph without refitting the model. The threshold should be justified and, preferably, specified before examining the results; it is not part of the EBIC selection procedure.

threshold_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "glasso", threshold = 0.1)
threshold_net
#> <psychnet> glasso network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 8   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.00861   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality: unavailable for post-threshold graph  (pre-threshold residual 2.21e-10)
as.data.frame(threshold_net)
#>   from to     weight
#> 1  CSU IV  0.4116687
#> 2  CSU SE  0.3829022
#> 3   IV SE  0.1599260
#> 4  CSU SR  0.3548136
#> 5   IV SR  0.3190944
#> 6   SE SR  0.2076721
#> 7   IV TA  0.1105874
#> 8   SR TA -0.3498516

At a threshold of 0.1, 8 edges remain. The CSU–TA (0.049) and SE–TA (0.099) edges are omitted, while the selected penalty remains unchanged. Because the thresholded graph is not itself the solution of the graphical-lasso objective, its optimality is reported as unavailable. The printout gives the pre-threshold residual (2.21×10−102.21 \times 10^{-10}), and certificate(threshold_net) returns NA. Reports should distinguish these post-hoc exclusions from edges set to zero during model estimation.

Do the conclusions depend on normality?

The GGM’s conditional-independence interpretation rests on multivariate normality. The nonparanormal model (Liu et al., 2009) relaxes it: each variable is mapped to normal scores through its ranks, and the same EBIC graphical lasso is fitted to the transformed data. method = "huge" fits this model.

npn_net <- psychnet(data = SRL_GPT, method = "huge")
summary(npn_net)
#> <psychnet> huge network
#>   nodes: 5   edges: 10   (undirected)
#>   lambda: 0.008559   gamma: 0.5
#>   optimality (KKT residual): 2.47e-10
#>   edge weight: range [-0.343, 0.426], mean 0.172
as.data.frame(npn_net)
#>    from to      weight
#> 1   CSU IV  0.42556520
#> 2   CSU SE  0.40615961
#> 3    IV SE  0.12908167
#> 4   CSU SR  0.34672549
#> 5    IV SR  0.31792725
#> 6    SE SR  0.19589994
#> 7   CSU TA  0.02390372
#> 8    IV TA  0.12511890
#> 9    SE TA  0.09634264
#> 10   SR TA -0.34267471
certificate(npn_net)
#>   method  certificate kind certified
#> 1   huge 2.471392e-10  kkt      TRUE

The nonparanormal fit retains all 10 edges, with weights from -0.343 to 0.426. Its certificate (2.47×10−102.47 \times 10^{-10}) satisfies the numerical optimality criterion. The six positive edges among the learning constructs remain, and the self-regulation to test anxiety edge is still negative (-0.343). The CSU–TA edge decreases from 0.049 in the Pearson-based GGM to 0.024. The principal pattern is therefore similar across these fits, but this comparison alone cannot establish that the assumptions hold or quantify the sampling stability of individual edges.

Reporting the analysis

A report states the variables and their measurement scale, the sample size, the correlation estimator, the treatment of missing data, the estimator and the value of γ\gamma, and any threshold. The edges are reported as partial correlations, with centrality and predictability defined before they are interpreted.

For these 300 complete, language-model-generated responses, an EBIC graphical lasso (γ=0.5\gamma = 0.5) based on Pearson correlations selected λ=0.00861\lambda = 0.00861 and retained all 10 possible edges. The largest positive partial correlation was between cognitive strategy use and intrinsic value (0.412), and the only negative partial correlation was between self-regulation and test anxiety (-0.350). The Spearman-based model retained 9 edges and the nonparanormal model retained 10; both preserved the positive learning-construct cluster and the negative self-regulation to test anxiety association. Changes in individual edge weights, particularly those involving test anxiety, should be reported rather than treated as evidence of exact replication.

Assumptions and when to use the GGM

  • The variables are continuous, or ordinal with enough categories to be treated as continuous; otherwise use polychoric correlations (cor_method = "auto"), the Ising model for binary data, or a mixed graphical model when continuous and binary variables are combined.
  • The joint distribution is approximately multivariate normal; the nonparanormal model is the sensitivity check when it is not.
  • Observations are independent. Repeated measures of the same persons call for a model that separates within- and between-person variation, such as the panel graphical VAR.
  • The regularized GGM suits analyses where a sparse, readable network is the goal. When the sample is large relative to the number of variables and unshrunk partial correlations are wanted, the stepwise model selection of method = "ggm" is the alternative.
  • An edge represents a conditional association, not a causal effect. A missing edge is an estimated zero in the selected model, not proof that the variables are unrelated in the population. Sampling uncertainty and the choice of estimation method remain important.

Mathematical details

Optimality conditions

Write 𝐖=𝐊̂−1\mathbf{W} = \widehat{\mathbf{K}}^{-1}. At the minimum of the graphical-lasso objective the diagonal satisfies Wii=SiiW_{ii} = S_{ii}, and for the off-diagonal entries

Wij−Sij=λsign⁡(K̂ij)if K̂ij≠0,|Wij−Sij|≤λif K̂ij=0. W_{ij} - S_{ij} = \lambda\,\operatorname{sign}(\widehat{K}_{ij}) \quad \text{if } \widehat{K}_{ij} \ne 0, \qquad |W_{ij} - S_{ij}| \leq \lambda \quad \text{if } \widehat{K}_{ij} = 0.

certificate() reports the largest violation of these conditions. For the strictly convex graphical-lasso objective, sufficiently small violations indicate that the numerical solution is close to the unique optimum. This assessment concerns optimisation rather than statistical uncertainty.

Selection of the penalty

The path holds candidate values of λ\lambda on a logarithmic grid. Each is fitted, the EBIC is computed, and the value with the smallest EBIC is refitted at a tighter numerical tolerance before it is returned.

Predictability

The residual variance of node jj given all other nodes is 1/Kjj1/K_{jj}. With marginal variance SjjS_{jj}, the explained proportion is

Rj2=1−1KjjSjj. R_j^2 = 1 - \frac{1}{K_{jj}S_{jj}}.
